intro: No ceremonial introduction: the accompaniment is already moving when the violin tune arrives. The same falling semitone supplies melody, transition and contrapuntal argument across this compact sonata movement.
question: What changes when the second theme returns in the minor?

relations.label: The opening returns in the recapitulation
relations.basis: The first-theme group returns in G minor after the development; the measured later span agrees with the recapitulation marked near 194 s. This performance omits the exposition repeat. CENS diagonal mean 0.972, sustained 22 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 193.5 s (cache/form/mozart-40-molto-allegro.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Already in motion
cues.text: The movement begins without a slow introduction. Listen for the opening melody’s repeated notes and small downward step against the moving accompaniment; a compact figure supplies material for much of the later argument.
cues.evidence: The score’s opening figure and its later development are discussed by Matthew Lorenzon for ABC Classic. This describes the opening passage rather than a timed violin entrance. https://www.abc.net.au/listen/classic/read-and-watch/music-reads/mozart-symphony-no-40-sonata-form/10160386
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The opening gains weight
cues.text: Across this stretch, the restrained opening gives way to stronger, busier writing. Listen for the contrast between a tune’s first presentation and the more forceful material that connects it to what follows.
cues.evidence: The report shows increasing relative level and more detected attacks around 0:25–0:40. It supports a broad change of texture, not an isolated entrance.

cues.title: A contrasting second theme
cues.text: The exposition’s second theme is in B♭ major, the relative major of G minor. Keep its chromatic, semitone-rich shape in mind: its later return will change the tonal setting without abandoning the recognisable line.
cues.evidence: Lorenzon describes the second theme and its altered return. The quieter passage after about 0:50 suggests its approximate location here; it is not aligned to the score.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Three symphonies in one summer
cues.text: Mozart composed his last three symphonies in the summer of 1788. The G minor symphony sits between No. 39 in E♭ major and No. 41 in C major; their sequence does not establish a private narrative programme.
cues.evidence: Marianne Williams Tobias’s Indianapolis Symphony note documents the summer sequence of Nos. 39–41. https://www.indianapolissymphony.org/backstage/program-notes/mozart-symphony-no-40/

cues.title: Developing a small fragment
cues.text: Through the development, listen for the first theme’s opening cell rather than a complete melody. Changing its key, register and companions lets Mozart make one small figure perform several different jobs.
cues.evidence: The score-based ABC guide describes the development’s use of the opening cell. A strong recorded change near 2:00 is consistent with its approximate position; the report alone cannot prove repeat practice.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Follow imitation across the parts
cues.text: In the central writing, try following one fragment as another part takes it up. Imitation can overlap statements instead of waiting for one line to finish before the next begins.
cues.evidence: The Indianapolis Symphony commentary identifies counterpoint in the development. The prompt does not assign a particular entry or instrument. https://www.indianapolissymphony.org/backstage/program-notes/mozart-symphony-no-40/
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A return with another task
cues.text: The recapitulation brings the main themes back, but changes the route between them. Compare familiar shapes with the earlier exposition rather than assuming the movement has simply restarted.
cues.evidence: Lorenzon describes the recapitulation and its expanded transition. The report’s change near 3:14 supports an approximate location, not a verified score-bar boundary.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The longer connecting passage
cues.text: The returning transition is longer than its earlier counterpart. Listen for familiar figures being worked further: a recapitulation can continue the process of development rather than merely reciting the themes.
cues.evidence: The expanded transition is documented in the ABC analysis. The active stretch around 3:45–4:20 is its estimated location in this performance, not a reviewed alignment.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The second theme in minor
cues.text: In the recapitulation, the second theme returns in G minor rather than B♭ major. Compare its melodic outline with its first presentation: bringing the theme home also changes its mode.
cues.evidence: The score and Lorenzon’s analysis establish the changed tonal setting. The quieter region after about 4:25 suggests where to compare it; the report’s key estimates alone do not establish the mode.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two orchestral versions
cues.text: Two versions of the symphony survive, one without clarinets and a later one with them. The revision is evidence of Mozart’s return to the score, not by itself proof of a particular first-performance occasion.
cues.evidence: The Indianapolis Symphony note distinguishes the two scorings and the uncertainty surrounding early performances. This recording’s version is not established here. https://www.indianapolissymphony.org/backstage/program-notes/mozart-symphony-no-40/

cues.title: One more closing insistence
cues.text: Across the ending, listen for a brief reduction in activity followed by renewed attacks. A pause in the pressure can strengthen the final gestures rather than signal that the movement is already over.
cues.evidence: The report detects fewer attacks around 5:35–5:40 and renewed activity around 5:45–5:50, followed by the final decay. No precise coda bar is assigned.

transitions.title: The dominant stops the argument
transitions.how: The forceful transition leaves G minor and gathers on F major, the dominant chord of B♭ major. Repeated orchestral emphasis on that harmony ends in a break: the medial caesura, a punctuation mark before the second theme. The bass’s F has prepared B♭, but the new phrase also changes the scale of the conversation. Quiet strings and woodwind exchange a chromatic, semitone-rich line instead of the preceding tutti’s driving figures. The tempo does not relax; longer notes and lighter scoring create the contrast.
transitions.evidence: Section boundary: Second theme, 50 s. The report marks a boundary at 0:50 and a relative-level fall from −8.3 dB at 0:40 to −23.5 dB at 0:50. The written transition closes on the dominant of B♭ before the quieter second subject; these harmonic and scoring claims come from the score, not the estimated key labels. The section timing is approximate.

transitions.title: B♭ major loses its footing
transitions.how: The exposition has established B♭ major through its closing cadences. Instead of continuing within that key, Mozart begins the development with the first theme in F♯ minor: a direct tonal displacement, not a smoothly prepared dominant–tonic arrival. The familiar repeated notes and falling semitone make the melody recognisable while its harmonic footing changes. Lighter string writing replaces the closing orchestral insistence; the theme will soon be broken into overlapping fragments and passed through further keys. Recognition and disorientation happen together.
transitions.evidence: Section boundary: Development, 120 s. The report’s strongest boundary is 2:00, where F♯, A and C♯ replace the preceding B♭-region material; this corroborates the score’s F♯ minor opening of the development. The relations file identifies this performance as omitting the exposition repeat. No pivot chord is inferred from chroma.

transitions.title: Fragments wait on D
transitions.how: After the development’s changing keys and overlapping entries, the harmony settles on D, the dominant of G minor. Holding that bass foundation turns the remaining fragments into preparation rather than another departure. The texture and force subside before the first theme regains its full phrase over the moving string accompaniment. D resolves to G; the original repeated-note figure and falling semitone now recover their opening tonal setting. The return is prepared by a prolonged dominant, not announced by a new tempo.
transitions.evidence: Section boundary: Recapitulation, 194 s. The report gives D-centred windows at 3:00–3:10, falling relative level, and a boundary at 3:14. The score supplies the dominant preparation and G minor thematic return. The provisional relations match at 197–219 s corroborates the returning opening but does not align the first bar.

transitions.title: The same pause leads to minor
transitions.how: Mozart lengthens and reworks the transition rather than copying its earlier route to B♭ major. This time the gathering point is D major, the dominant of G minor, and another break releases the second theme into the home key. Its semitone-inflected outline and exchanges between strings and woodwind remain recognisable, but B♭, the minor third above the tonic G, prevents the exposition’s major-key ease from returning unchanged. The bass and cadence have redirected a familiar phrase; this is not simply the whole melody transposed down three semitones.
transitions.evidence: Section boundary: Second theme returns, 265 s. Relative level falls from −8.6 dB at 4:20 to −22.9 dB at 4:25, with D prominent across the join. The score establishes the expanded transition, D-dominant preparation and second subject in G minor; the relations file explicitly warns that its mode change is not a uniform transposition. Timing remains approximate.

composer.background:
Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, the seventh child of Leopold Mozart and Anna Maria Pertl; only he and his sister Maria Anna survived infancy. Leopold was a violinist and composer in the archbishop’s service, and in the year of Wolfgang’s birth published an influential violin treatise. He taught both children. Maria Anna, called Nannerl within the family, became an accomplished keyboard player, and the first tours presented brother and sister together. The family’s travels were an educational system as well as a business: the children encountered instruments, performers, repertories and audiences that a Salzburg childhood alone could not have supplied.

The long tour of 1763–66 took them through German courts, Paris, London and the Netherlands. In London Mozart met Johann Christian Bach, whose clear phrases and Italianate melodic style offered a model different from the contrapuntal teaching associated with Bach’s father. Illness repeatedly interrupted the itinerary. Leopold managed engagements, publicity and money while supervising composition, and the surviving correspondence documents the costs and uncertainties behind the public demonstrations. Wolfgang learned to write for named performers and immediate occasions before he had an independent adult household.
composer.epithet: An opera composer whose instrumental music gives different voices the freedom to disagree.
